newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks, bonds rise on Greenspan comments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks, bonds rise on Greenspan comments.

text.p: U.S. stocks bounced higher and bonds rallied early on Friday after comments by Alan Greenspan assuaged fears over the near-term outlook for interest rates.

But stocks quickly relinquished their opening gains as enthusiasm over Greenspan's comments gave way to caution that the Fed chairman, as always, stopped well short of tipping his hand on upcoming policy.
"I did detect a little crack in his resolve and I suspect this next (Fed) meeting will have some debate," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter.
"But people have to remember that this is a two-handed economist and the last thing he wants to do is commit to anything, particularly in public," he added.

Analysts expressed little doubt that investors initially viewed Greenspan's comments bullishly. The Dow industrials burst 52 points higher to 7189 in the opening minutes, but shed all but a dozen points of those gains.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury rose 23/32, trimming the yield to 6.88 percent, only to give back about a third of its winnings.
Some analysts warned the market's early rally masked an elevated degree of risk heading into the Fed's May 20 interest rate policy meeting.
In contrast to the March meeting, which resulted in a widely-anticipated 25 basis point rate increase, analysts said Wall Street appeared unprepared for a follow-up move.

"It has been our house call that the Fed will raise rates on May 20," said Douglas Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at J.P. Morgan. "That makes us cautious, because we don't think that's priced into the market with the S&P 500 priced at 820."
However, a resurgent optimism, which carried blue chips to record levels early this week for the first time since March, was a sign the warnings were going unheeded, analysts said.

"I candidly believe that although the economists and strategists had been split, the markets had been sending a very clear message that investors did not expect the Fed to raise rates," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.
For those still expecting a rate move, the rallying U.S. financial markets ahead of expected Fed rate increases meant risks outweighed potential rewards at this point.

"We continue to believe Chairman Greenspan is predisposed to tighten further," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "That's one reason we've been raising a little cash here."
For those looking beyond the next meeting, a decision by the Fed not to act in May could trigger some asset shifting and a mixed response from stocks and bonds as investors adjust their outlooks.
"That would mean (the Fed) has a greater tolerance for a stronger economy and I think the bond market has been trained to react negatively to strength," Canelo said.
Stocks, on the other hand, would continue to benefit from the expected earnings growth that accompanies a strong economy, he said.
